speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That a message be sent to the Senate that this house agrees with all the Senate amendments to Bill No. 40, an act to provide for minimum wages pursuant to the convention concerning minimum wages adopted by the International Labour Organization in accordance with the provisions of part XIII of the treaty of Versailles and of the corresponding parts of the other treaties of peace, and that the Clerk of the House do carry the said message to the Senate.

That we agree to all the
amendments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What are they?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They have rewritten part of the bill. If hon. gentlemen so desire I shall be glad to point out what the changes are.
The provisions of the preamble have not been changed, nor has section 1. But on pages 2, 3 and 4 it will be observed that the sections have been entirely recast, down to the end of section 8. The effect is that the section has been tied closely to the terms of the convention. The law officers of the Senate thought it advisable, and the Senate committee agreed, that the terms used in the convention should be reproduced, for the purpose of dealing with, for instance, rateable

Minimum Wage-Senate Amendments
trades and matters of that sort. It will be observed on the page opposite page 2 that words that were not defined in the bill as it left the house have been defined in accordance with the terms of the convention. Some of the changes are very slight but others are quite substantial. Section 3 is recast. Section 4 permits the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister to create, and by regulation provide for the operation of, machinery with respect to minimum wages. Section 5 is recast, and in section 6 there is quite a change. You will observe particularly words to which attention anight be directed as having been added :
the trade and commerce, or the public revenue, of Canada is being injuriously-affected by the absence of uniform minimum rates of wages,
That has been added by the Senate. The words that have been used in section 5 and other sections, "decent standard" have been taken out and the words "suitable standard"
' substituted. It seems to me that perhaps that is an improvement. Those are the essential changes that have been made, in substance, and the recasting has continued, as will be observed opposite page 4. I think I should direct the attention of the house to the last section opposite the end of page 4:
Subsection one of section four of this act and section five of this act shall not come into force until proclaimed by the governor in council.
I think I explained when this bill was before the house originally that it does not come into force until the time limited, because the convention itself did not become operative merely by ratification-I will read the article in order that there may be no difficulty. Article 7 provides:
This convention shall be binding only upon those members whose ratifications have been registered with the secretariat.
It shall come into force twelve months after the date on which the ratifications of two members of the international labour organization have been registered with the secretary-general.
I pointed out that this happened, of course, before the convention was submitted to this house. The last paragraph of article 7 is the governing paragraph:
Thereafter, this convention shall come into force for any member twelve months after the date on which its ratification has been registered.
Our ratification was registered on the 25th day of April, 1935; therefore the convention does not come into force until twelve months after that date. The amendment made by the senate provides that subsection 1 of section 4
and section 5 shall not come into force until proclaimed by the governor in council, in order that the full twelve months may expire after ratification before the proclamation is made with respect to those provisions that are tied up to the convention itself.
Does that mean a year from now at least?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Substantially; April 25, 1936, to be exact. That is why it is provided that a proclamation is to be made, in order that the full year may have expired before it comes into force. That refers to section 5 as rewritten and to the provisions of subsection 1 of section 4, and in order that there may be no difficulty about it I will read that subsection:
4.	(1) The governor in council may on the recommendation of the minister create, and by regulation provide for the operation by or under the minister of, machinery whereby minimum rates of wages can be fixed for workers employed in rateable trades.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved the second reading of Bill No. 99, respecting radio broadcasting.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before second reading is given to the bill I should like to make a few observations on the radio situation in Canada and the circumstances which have led this government to ask parliament to reenact the provisions of the Radio Broadcasting Act of 1932 for a further period of nine months, thereby extending the life of the commission to the end of the fiscal year.
When we studied the problem we did not have to make a decision of principle, because that question was settled in 1932 when the house unanimously decided that radio broadcasting in Canada should become a, public utility. The statute, it is well to bear in mind, was enacted after the report of the Aird-Frigon commission which was organized by the administration of hon. members opposite and the report of the committee headed by the Deputy Speaker, both of which recommended and advocated the public ownership of radio. I am not aware, Mr. Speaker, of any change in the attitude or views of the great majority of the members of this house or of any change in public opinion as to the principle of the public ownership of radio. The principle of public ownership was also affirmed by the special committee which reported last session when special recommendations were made to the house. If the house will permit me to quote the first recommendation of that committee, it reads as follows:
That in view of the evidence given before this committee the government should during the recess consider the advisability of amending the act with a view to securing better broadcasting facilities throughout the dominion, [n the opinion of your committee radio broadcasting could best be conducted by a general manager.
As the house can see, the report did not even touch or raise the question of principle. The only question brought to the attention of the government was about the organization and the management of this utility. I can assure this house that the government has given most careful consideration to the report made by that committee, and after careful study we came to the conclusion that as we were nearing the end of the present parliament we should not interfere with the principle or with the organization of the commission at the present time. There is no

doubt that this problem of radio in Canada is a very important one, but we thought that it was not urgent enough to come and ask the house at this session for drastic legislation amending the organization of the commission.
I think that in fairness to the personnel of the commission I should bring some considerations before the house concerning the commission's achievements. I think every member of this house will agree that the commission was entrusted with a very, very difficult task, a task that was somewhat in the nature of an experiment not only in Canada but all over the continent of America. The commission has hardly been two years in office, which is indeed a very short period within which to test the value of the system. Every member of the house I think will also admit that the commission has been further handicapped by the lack of funds. Nobody could expect the commission to build a network to cover half this continent, a network as complete as they have in Great Britain, in less than three years without any capital other than its appropriation of about one million dollars a year. In those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think that the record of the Canadian radio commission has been a creditable one.
I know that the commission has been very bitterly criticized from almost all sections of the country and I am frank to admit that many of the criticisms were well founded, but I think I should add immediately that those who voiced the criticisms did not allow for the handicaps under which the commission had to operate. The complaints against our present system were listed under two headings, coverage and programs. If hon. members will give me their attention for a few minutes I 3hall endeavour to give them an idea of what the commission has already tried: to accomplish in spite of difficulties and limitations to improve the broadcasting facilities and provide better 'Canadian programs.
The objective assigned to the commission by parliament was the setting up of a national network built around three or four powerful stations, and the taking over of all private stations in Canada except the small or what we call the community stations. That undertaking everybody will admit involved considerable expenditure which the commission could not afford to make under the circumstances, with the meagre credits which were placed at their disposal. The commission has nevertheless managed to establish a network of its own which comprises seven stations

Radio Broadcasting-Mr. Duranleau
situated at strategic points throughout the country, namely, stations 'CRCV, Vancouver; CRCW, Windsor; CRCT, Toronto; CRCO, Ottawa; CRQM, Montreal; CRCK, Quebec; CRCS, Chicoutimi.

I am told that the commission is working to-day on a program of construction which it intends to carry out with the more generous allowance which we have voted this year and which, will help to increase the coverage all over Canada.
The commission has further improved broadcasting facilities by granting licences to small stations which operate in districts where there was no coverage before.
I know that some hon. members of this house ha?e criticized the commission because of the fact that the number of private stations has increased since the commission has been in operation, but the commission had not the necessary funds to establish its own stations, and in order to give better coverage to different parts of Canada t'he commission thought it well to issue private licences. I might mention in that connection the new stations at Prince Albert in northern Saskatchewan, at Sudbury in northern Ontario, at Sault Ste. Marie, Hull, New Carlisle on the Gaspe coast, and Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. The commission's programs are supplied without cost to all the private stations all over Canada.
May I add that the commission has carried out so far as possible the recommendations of the special committee of last session with respect to advertising, in which connection a more liberal interpretation was given by the commission as suggested by the report of the committee. The private stations were allowed to carry advertising for as much as fifteen per cent of their time.

Moreover, the private stations were permitted to use electrical transcriptions until 7.30 at night and even later in some cases. The commission has also endeavoured to cooperate with the private stations and assist them in every possible way in accordance with the fifth recommendation of the special committee. I do not intend to enter into any discussion in connection with programs as that is a matter of taste and personal preference. However, I will venture to say that the commission has provided us with distinctly Canadian programs of a higher quality and wider variety than we could have expected from our private stations with their limited resources. Besides the regular news and weather forecast services we have had opera, chamber and choral music, drama, educational talks covering a wide range of subjects and introducing the leaders in all fields of Canadian activity to the whole nation, band concerts, instrumental and vocal recitals, book reviews, news comments, children's programs, dance music, sports broadcasts and so forth. I am sure the establishment of our publicly owned radio system will have a far-reaching influence upon the future of music and drama in Canada. The commission has already discovered a good many Canadian artists of whom we may be proud and we may expect that it will encourage and help our gifted young Canadians. In the past there have been many gifted Canadians. I need mention only Edward Johnson who has been recently honoured. Artists like him might have been induced to establish themselves in Canada if an opportunity had been offered by such a radio system as we have now.
Another point which I wish to stress is the importance of the national service rendered by the Canadian radio broadcasting commission, as was demonstrated by the special broadcast on May 6 on the occasion of the silver jubilee of His Majesty the King. I am sure the house realizes that the credit for the Canadian participation in that extraordinary broadcast is diue to the Canadian radio broadcasting commission. I am told that the commission asks the same rate for political addresses as for ordinary commercial service. I do not think that is fair. It ought at least to be possible to give a lower rate fo>r the expression of opinions of candidates and especially of the leaders during the election, not the same rates as for advertising syrup and drugs and other goods. On a former occasion when radio was before the house I asked to wbat extent the recommendations of the committee of last year had been implemented. I understand they have not been.
I think at that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) promised a reply at a later day.
I raise the question to-day because I was impressed' with the fairness and strength of his statement at that time in regard to public ownership and the necessity for maintaining the principle. Since then it has come to my attention that there is a serious trend now developing in radio broadcasting in this country, a trend that affects stations of smaller power that may be leased to private owners. I am informed that there is a tendency towards the amalgamation or at least the leasing to chain companies of more and more of these privately owned low powered stations with, consequently, the quiet, steady growth of monopolies among these low powered stations. I do know of some illustrations of joint ownership, or single ownership, of a number of these stations; for example, the stations at North Bay, Kirkland Lake and Timmins are all owned by the same company or are all under the same general management. I think that is something that should be avoided, and I strongly recommend to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine that if the regulations can be amended to protect the principle of public ownership against this danger of a growing private monopoly among the small, low powered stations, it should be done. If it cannot be done by regulation then an amendment to the act should be passed. I suggest to the government that one way of meeting the difficulty would be to have a provision in the licence prohibiting the leasing of the station by the person or company securing the licence to construct and operate the station; in other words, that the right granted in the licence should not be transferable. In that way we would maintain the individual element in the operation of the low powered stations. Otherwise there is a serious danger in the general trend at the present time towards monopoly. I hope the Prime Minister will be able to amplify the statement he made the other evening.

speechtext:
I was going to say that in England that difficulty is negligible. There they have a compact population, and they told me they had seven million licences outstanding. Here to carry a broadcast across the country involves large expenditure for the use of the wire. The commission itself has no wires of any great length, it has stations, as the minister has explained, but to connect all those stations and amplify the broadcast so that it may be carried with sufficient strength and power to all parts of the country involves large expenditures. Our rates do look very high, but when you come to think that it is three thousand miles from Ottawa to Vancouver you realize why they have to be, the commission having no facilities of their own. As I say, they have to use the facilities which they lease for that purpose, and that is where the expenditure comes in.
As the minister observed, the real fact is that there is a very earnest desire on the part of the commission to provide the country with better broadcasting facilities. To do so involves the expenditure of large sums of money for a high powered station in each province; perhaps not one in each province but at least seven high powered stations. They cost a good deal of money, and the equipment connected with them also costs a good deal of money. The funds of the commission are limited entirely to their receipts from the use of their facilities and the money received in licence fees. It is much more expensive than it would appear to operate these broadcasting stations.

The only thing I was going to add to what the minister has said was that I brought back with me a copy of the report made by Sir John Reith on the situation in South Africa. They have decided to nationalize their broadcasting system and to establish the requisite number of stations. I brought the report with me intending to read some of the recommendations, but I find it unnecessary to do so now in view of what has been said.
I can only add that there is a great deal of sound reason in what the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has said, because it is quite clear that numbers of small stations owned by the same firm or individual may create a sort of monopoly that will prevent the commission itself from discharging its full functions. But the power that rests in the radio act makes it perfectly clear that all these licences are issued subject to the overriding right of expropriation. There is one thing further: In consequence of certain information that reached me I ascertained upon inquiry that all new licences have been issued subject to the condition that the state may take over the facilities and that no value attaches for good will or franchise, that it is merely the value of the physical equipment whatever that may be. That is my understanding from the answer I received to my inquiry. It makes it much simpler if there is no franchise value attached and obviously one of the difficulties to which reference has been made disappears.
I do not see how the commission, with its limited revenues and its difficulty in making ends meet, can possibly expect to provide facilities for any of us on the terms suggested by the ex-Minister of Justice. It cannot afford to do so; that is the difficulty. Of course the British Broadcasting Corporation, while it is criticized as all corporations are, has had such public support behind it because of the character of its programs that one realizes that it fills a very long felt want on those islands. But you must remember that there are seven million licences outstanding and that the state receives all but 4s. 6d. of the 10s. 6d. received for a licence, and that on the 4s. 6d. plus the advertising, the sale of their programs and their recordings they are able to make a very substantial sum of money. Broadcasting House, the building they have erected at the end of Oxford street, is a magnificent property. It contains great concert halls; they have made provision for Sunday services; they can carry on several programs at the same time, and they have installed every modern device. Notwithstanding that, from time to time they are endeavouring to improve their facilities, as this service always must be im-

Radio Broadcasting
proved. Just take one thing, the question of recordings. That is a modem development. It is possible for my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice to make a speech on the radio at ten o'clock this morning, 'and at the appropriate hour this evening it can be broadcast as though it were being delivered by him at the very moment it is being heard. The perfection of these recordings is a matter now of common knowledge. The progress that has been made in connection with these matters is most marvellous. Last night the governor general designate was being heard in this country very clearly; I suppose many members of the house heard him, speaking in England. When we think of the progress that has been made it really is amazing, and I do not think we have yet reached the end. Senator Marconi tells how warm a place in his heart he has for Canada, because the first signal he transmitted across the Atlantic ocean was largely made possible by the final help that was given him foy this country. I fancy the right hon. gentleman opposite has personal knowledge of the statements I am making. He told me that had it not 'been for the assistance he received from Canada upon that occasion it is doubtful whether or not he would have been able to complete his experiment. When we reflect that the first signal transmitted across the Atlantic ocean from Newfoundland to Poldhu in Cornwall was largely through the confidence that Canada had in his ability to do so, and when we compare that first signal with what we have to-day, I believe we have some reason for satisfaction. In these days we can transmit wireless sounds across the Atlantic ocean with great facility. I understand on the sixth of May those sounds were transmitted in. such a way that every person in Canada, either at a radio station or in his own house, could hear what was taking place in England. The electrical reproduction of it in the evening made it available to those who might have found it inconvenient to listen to the program as it was originally transmitted.	_
All these things cost money-vast sums of money. The only complaint I have ever had to offer was that possibly there was a tendency to be unduly critical of the very difficult position in which the commissioners first found themselves when they took over the organization of this great public utility, in the face of opposition of private owners. I say, and every man must know, that many of the privately owned stations were bitter in their denunciation of the publicly owned facilities, feeling that what would have been a profitable field in the future had been taken from them. They felt that while their property had not been
confiscated they were prevented' from carrying out that which they believed would have been a highly profitable venture in the future. That difficulty was encountered and I believe to some extent, overcome. I have not been blind to the fact however that there has been an insidious campaign going on for the purpose of endeavouring to destroy the public facility from the standpoint of public approval of its operation. Hon. gentlemen may have no idea of the extent to which it was urged upon the government that the time would come when radio would cease to be operated as a public facility and be turned over to private enterprise.
We have not felt warranted in asking parliament for any sum of money beyond that derived from licence fees. The fact is that in a country such as ours, with enormous distances and a very limited number of licences, the record of the commission is something for which we have some reason to be proud. Mr. Graves, of the British Broadcasting Corporation., who was in Ottawa a short time ago, told me he had no idea we had done so much. When he saw the great distance over which the commission had to operate; when he realized the difficulties in connection with land lines and limited appropriations, small population and small number of licences, travelling from here to Halifax he expressed very great interest in what we were doing and voiced the belief that upon his return to 'Great Britain he would more clearly understand our difficulties than he had hoped when he left that country. He is the gentleman responsible for what are known as empire programs of the British Broadcasting Corporation. I suppose every hon. member knows that a substantial number of people from the old country have found homes in western 'Canada and have taken the greatest possible interest in the empire programs broadcast by the British Broadcasting Corporation. I was told the other day by the manager that the letters he had received from western Canada with regard to the type of program transmitted across the Atlantic ocean and reaching the far western parts of Canada had interested and amazed him.
Although this is a day of small things, Mr. Chairman, I believe we have reason to congratulate ourselves upon the fact that we have retained this facility as the property of the people and' that for the moment there has been no weakening on the part of those charged with the responsibility in their determination to maintain it as a publicly owned facility. Although the future may demand expenditures on a more generous scale than
Radio Broadcasting

we have heretofore been able to provide, I am satisfied that more and more the demand for this facility will continue, and that if we pursue, shall I say, the steady course that we are following, we will in Canada develop a system of broadcasting of which the Canadian people may well in every sense be truly proud1.
I repeat, this is a day of small things, and at times we are apt to compare our requirements, if that word may be used, with- those which can be provided by very rich and powerful peoples. We cannot erect stations costing many hundreds of thousands of dollars. We cannot provide all the facilities some of (he privately owned corporations provide, but quietly, gradually and steadily we are improving the situation. I would say to the hon-. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) that one of the matters with which the commission has been most concerned has been the difficulty of securing adequate coverage in the province of British Columbia. The hon. member, who is so familiar with the coast line and the sparse population scattered throughout the northern part of British Columbia and in the interior, and who is aware that a great part of the population is to be found in the cities of Vancouver and Victoria, will realize that with the limited revenues derived from licence fees the maintenance in the sparsely settled areas of a service such as is maintained in the more thickly populated communities is almost impossible. However the commission is most anxious to erect a station at a point which will provide ample coverage for the whole of British Columbia.
In the prairies they have had many difficulties to meet, largely on account of the large number of small stations. The combination about which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) spoke is not lacking in that country. Although I had not intended to speak, I believe I might say to my fellow Canadians that comparing our facilities with those offered in the older and richer countries I believe Canadians, with the limited amount of money at their disposal, the difficulties in connection with organizing a sendee of this kind, and the further difficulty sometimes brought about by the use of two languages, may well be proud. All these factors enter into broadcasting difficulties. Because of our great area we have time changes at Fort William, again at Broadview and again at Field. Then we have to make allowance for ' daylight saving. These are factors which do not enter into broadcasting in a country such as Great Britain!, but they are factors which must nevertheless be considered. The de-

velopment of a system, for instance, which makes it possible for us to hear a concert in London is not an easy procedure, because there is a difference of five hours in time. Then there are certain adjustments necessary, difficulties in atmospheric changes, and the power of appliances required to move the signal away beyond the ether and the stratosphere so that it may cross the ocean and then be gathered together and reproduced in Canada. These are processes which are almost miraculous. Radio is one of those things which one can never thoroughly understand, and something which to the average person is as near a miracle as anything we know in the world to-day.
I do hope, as the days go by, whatever government is in office may see to it that there are some sort of, shall I say, expressions of approval wherever possible of the earnest effort that is being made to secure and maintain, and that these will not be lacking on the part of those holding positions such as we hold. I trust that the tendency to criticize and condemn, which is not always without some cause, will become less and less. Approval of earnest efforts to provide the people of Canada, despite limited revenues and great physical and other difficulties, will be duly and properly appreciated.

I find myself in pretty general agreement with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has just said respecting the general working of the radio commission. I am not altogether content with the assurance that the radio commission will have power or has power now to check any monopolistic development. The fact is I want them to exercise that power. I am informed, for example, that a very strong and financially important company, the General Electric, is at the present time preparing the organization of a holding company with which it proposes to control a large chain of now privately owned stations. In the last year or two there has of course been a very rapid increase, in my opinion too rapid an increase, in the number of licences issued to small private stations. I would have preferred to see that licensing limited to a much greater degree than it has been, but we are now faced with that tendency, and if it is permitted to continue unchecked, in spite of the provision to which the Prime Minister referred, you are eventually going to have a claim based on vested rights which it would be very difficult for this house and for the members of any government to overcome. In connection with fines, it will be noticed that section 18 provides for a fine of not less than one hundred dollars. That seems to be an excessive penalty for a small offence. The Prime Minister to-day referred to an amendment made by the Senate to a certain bill in which a minimum penalty was cut out, and it was only $25. He suggested that it was held by many people to be desirable not to have a minimum penalty, and here we have a minimum of $100 for a trivial offence. Is this in the old act? In any event that would not justify such an excessive penalty. The minister is aware that the imposition of heavy minimum penalties very often prejudices magistrates in favour of offenders; they would rather let them off than impose an unjust penalty.

The hon. gentleman will remember that a year ago, when this bill was before the house, this very matter was discussed at great length, though I realize, of course, that this is not an answer to his argument. All these penalties are named by the Department of Justice, and $100 is not really a very large fine to be paid by those who would be concerned, if the act is to have any effect at all.

The penalties are provided for in connection with sections 10, 11 and 12. Section 10 deals with the commission agent who has neglected to obtain a licence,, and that is not a deadly offence. Section 11 provides that no dealer shall ship, buy, accept or offer to accept or otherwise deal in any produce shipped unless he has obtained a licence; and section 12 provides that no broker shall engage in negotiating shipments on consignment, sales or purchases of any produce, and so on, without having obtained a licence. These are not vicious offences; I can think of offences which are much more
serious and for which the minimum is less than 8100. The minister says cheerfully that $100 is not much. It depends on whose pocket it comes out of; I know people who would have to go to gaol for a trivial offence for a period not exceeding two months if they were required to pay a fine of $100. I do suggest that $100 is a drastic penalty. The minister says that the Department of Agriculture prescribed it. Yes, and I have always noticed that the Department of Agriculture more than any other department is very strong on that-imposing the most excessive penalties for the infringement of any act or regulation they are pleased to make. That department is particularly guilty in this respect. They seem to think that if a man does anything contrary to a regulation on which they have put their imprimatur he should be crucified, on the principle, I suppose, of the Turkish sultan who put a dishonest baker in his oven. But that is not the principle that applies to-day; now we try to make the penalty fit the offence. I do not believe that if the matter were left to the minister himself, who is a fairminded man, he would deny that $100 is an excessive minimum penalty for offences like these. To test the point I move that in section 18, in line 37, the words "one hundred dollars" be struck out and the words "twenty-five dollars" be substituted therefor.

The fine set out
in section 18 applies to the offences dealt with in sections 10, 11 and 12, on the basis of failure to take out a licence. The taking out of a licence is the basis on which an important part of this bill rests. If the hon. gentleman will read section 19 he will see the penalties enumerated for the smaller offences he has in mind. Before the bill was brought in last year, all these sections had been given consideration for at least eighteen months and had been before the fruit growers' associations in Canada. Some of them had it in their hands for a year. They went into the matter fully and were of the opinion that, because of the importance and the necessity of the licence being insisted upon, the fine should be at least $100. The hon. gentleman would give the impression that the Department of Agriculture is particularly desirous of imposing penalties, but I may tell him that I know of no instance where a penalty had been imposed without at least three warnings. To adopt the hon. member's suggestion would mean that the bill would not be effective. It is felt that it would be more satisfactory to leave it as it is, taking care that no injustice should be done through oversight.

Would the minister then
agree to add at the end of the section the provision that no such fine shall be imposed until a man has received at least three warnings? That, he says, is the basis of the bill.

No; I did not say
that the basis of it was the giving of three warnings; I said that was the policy of the department, and it shows that the department is not anxious to impose fines. The hon. gentleman would be the first to agree that to make the change he suggests would render the bill ineffective with respect to one or two convictions.

The language is so vague:
No commission agent shall accept or offer to accept for sale on commission ...
The licence may have expired two days before and he may have sent his money to Ottawa; it has not arrived and he is liable. And it is not a matter of his being liable for $100; he is liable for 81,000. Why $1,000? It is all very well to say that the department is not in the habit of being unjust in prosecutions. Possibly not. But why give them such extraordinary powers? Why make the penalties so exorbitant? Half the time the accused will get off, because no reasonable justice of the peace or magistrate will fine a man $100 for a trivial offence. It is the experience of all magistrates that an excessive penalty for a minor offence is always provocative of undue leniency. It is in the interests of the enforcement of the act that I suggest making the penalties reasonable. If they are reasonable there is a better chance of the act being enforced. It is not the terrible penalty that deters a man but the certainty of conviction. Make the officers do their duty and see that every infraction of the act is brought to court. That is the thing that stops it, not the idea that he can take a chance. He may be fined $1,000 or may get off altogether, but it is the certainty of conviction that counts. I suggest that $100 is too much for a mistake of that kind. I would like to go further and reduce the maximum from $1,000 to $500, but I would not press that if the minister would agree to the $100.

This matter was before the committee last year. I think the reason this particular penalty was inserted was to protect the producer. As I read the statute, no person can act as commission agent for these products unless he secures a licence. I do not understand that this licence will1 be

renewable from time to time; there is no provision for that. I submit that in order to control these parties effectively and protect the producers it is necessary to licence the commission people who will be taking these goods for sale on commission, and if they have not a licence they should be subject to a substantial penalty. I see no objection to this legislation; in fact I would support it because of the protection it gives the producers.

Can the minister inform us how long these fines have been in force, how' many prosecutions have been entered and how many convictions obtained', and whether he has found any difficulty from the courts hesitating about convicting because of the large fines? That would help to guide us in our decision. There is no question that when a fine is unreasonable-I am not saying this is-there is difficulty in securing convictions. If the minister would give us his experience of the eases that have been brought to court it -would help us.

This has been in force for one year. There have been no prosecutions, therefore no fines have been imposed to date. The licence is $25 and if the fine were reduced to $25 it might; be a temptation to some to take a chance.

My recollection is that on the introduction of any new legislation like this the practice of the Department of Agriculture is to admonish and warn transgressors rather than prosecute much for the first year. Now that year is over; what will be the policy next year? The department will be disposed to be a little more severe, I imagine. If it is not, some will simply go on and on offending to see how much the minister will stand for. I am not disposed to suggest any change here.	I have no doubt the
officers of the department have gone into it carefully and fully and have decided that these fines seem to be workable, and fair, because there is no use having laws unless they are enforced. But when it is broken through ignorance rather than deliberately there should be some consideration shown, and there usually is.

There is just one other point to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister. In the event of the validity of the act appointing a trade and industry commission being questioned and it being found that the act in any particular is ultra vires, then there would be no combines investigation act in force at all. I was going to ask the government if it had considered the advisability of inserting some clause providing that in the event of the validity of the trade and industry commission act being questioned and that measure being found invalid, the old combines act might be forthwith revived.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid a clause of that kind would be considered a confession of weakness on the part of the government. I may say that in the view of the government the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act is constitutional; all the legal opinion we have been able to get on it has been to the effect that it is intra vires.
